solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Star players given gold

parts.note: the players in a production are its cast
or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: Top performers in a show receive gold awards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star players' reads as one phrase about celebrities, but 'Star' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Castor is one of the twin bright stars in the constellation Gemini, beside Pollux.

clue.text: Spooner's prohibited string as stuff for packagers

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the initial sounds of two words trade places

parts.note: prohibited is barred and string is cord; swap the opening sounds

explanation.surface: A banned kind of twine used by people who wrap parcels.
explanation.definitionFit: Cardboard is the stiff pasteboard material that boxes and packing are made from.

clue.text: Describing shock of aimless drifting

indicators.note: drifting letters wander out of place and settle in a new order

parts.note: the fodder, every letter used

explanation.surface: An account of the trauma of wandering without purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shock' reads as emotional, but it is an earthquake shock; the definition is an adjective phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Seismal is a rare variant of seismic, the adjective for earthquakes and their tremors.

clue.text: Letters in some message mostly taken the wrong way

indicators.note: taken the wrong way means read in the opposite direction, right to left
in some says the letters sit inside part of the text that follows

parts.note: the run of letters spanning the two words, read before turning

explanation.surface: Text in a message mostly misunderstood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' looks like an instruction to trim a word, but it is part of the hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: Omega is the last letter of the Greek alphabet, so omegas are letters.

clue.text: Chum protecting artist, thus providing cover

indicators.note: to protect something is to shield it on every side, so one piece wraps around the others

parts.note: a chum is a friend or pal
RA is a Royal Academician, the usual crossword artist
so means in this way, thus

explanation.surface: A friend shields a painter, and so gives them protection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Providing cover' reads as protection from the friend; it is a noun phrase for a sunshade.
explanation.definitionFit: A parasol is a sunshade, which is a thing providing cover from the sun; the definition is read as a noun phrase.

clue.text: Quiet advocate for a flushing out of the old order?

definitions.text: flushing out of the old order?

parts.note: p, piano, is the musical mark for quiet
to advocate is to urge

explanation.surface: A soft-spoken voice calling for the old guard to be removed.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is loose: a purge removes old members of a party or regime.
explanation.definitionFit: A purge is the abrupt removal of unwanted people from an organisation, a clearing out of the establishment.

clue.text: Pole should be freer — too tight

indicators.note: tight is slang for drunk, and drunk letters reel into a new arrangement

parts.note: fodder, taken as written
fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A Polish person complains about restrictions being too tight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' reads as a person from Poland; it is a beam. 'Tight' looks like a contrast to freer but is the drunk anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A rooftree is the ridgepole, the horizontal beam along the top of a roof.

clue.text: Hamper in hut left half abandoned

indicators.note: half of the word is abandoned, so only part of it remains

parts.note: a shack is a hut
taken as written; its second half goes

explanation.surface: A picnic basket left behind in a deserted cabin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hamper' reads as a basket; it is the verb. 'In' only joins definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To shackle someone is to restrict or impede them, as to hamper does.

clue.text: Hotelier has this — it may be associated with room service for breakfast?

definitions.text: it may be associated with room service for breakfast?

parts.note: these three letters sit inside the hotel keeper's title, from its sixth letter
this points to the fact itself: the three letters are in the word, so describe them as being in

explanation.surface: A hotel offers late mornings with breakfast brought to the room.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue states where the short word sits: it is IN hoteLIEr, and that statement reads as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A lie-in is a late stay in bed in the morning, when guests might order breakfast to the room.

clue.text: Hopeful type with venom, I rave

parts.note: an asp is a venomous snake
taken as written
to rave is to rant

explanation.surface: A spiteful wannabe shouting angrily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hopeful type' reads as one phrase, but the definition is 'Hopeful' alone, as a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: An aspirant is someone who aspires to a goal, a hopeful in the noun sense of candidate.

clue.text: Commendation, when leader leaves, brings uplift

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, and it leaves, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: praise is commendation

explanation.surface: Praise from a departing boss gives the staff a lift.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the P from PRAISE to leave RAISE.
explanation.definitionFit: To raise something is to lift it up, so raise and uplift are synonyms as verbs or nouns.

clue.text: Agent certain to carry round gun after end of war

indicators.note: something that carries a load holds it within, so one word goes around the rest

parts.note: certain means sure

indicators.note: after says the following piece is placed later in the run of letters
'end of' keeps only the last letter of 'war'

parts.note: the last letter of war
a round shape is the letter O
gat is old slang for a gun

explanation.surface: A secret agent is sure to pack a pistol once the war is over.
explanation.walkthrough: Gat is old American gangster slang for a pistol, from Gatling gun.
explanation.definitionFit: A surrogate is a deputy who acts on behalf of another, which is what an agent does.

clue.text: A lot of money offered by a specialist mag for material

parts.note: a bomb is British slang for a large sum of money
taken as written
a zine is a small specialist or fan magazine

explanation.surface: A fat fee paid by a niche magazine for an article.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Material' looks like written copy for the magazine; it is cloth. 'Cost a bomb' is British for costing a fortune.
explanation.definitionFit: Bombazine is a twilled dress fabric of silk and worsted, once common for mourning clothes.

clue.text: Number receiving satisfactory sign

indicators.note: a word receiving another takes it in, so it surrounds those letters

parts.note: ten is a number
OK means satisfactory

explanation.surface: A number gets a thumbs-up mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A token is a sign or symbol of something, as in a token of esteem.

clue.text: Silly fellow ignoring wife or partner

indicators.note: to ignore something is to leave it out, so a letter is removed

parts.note: a wally is British slang for a silly person
W is the abbreviation for wife, and it is the letter dropped

explanation.surface: A foolish man who neglects his wife, or his partner.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove W from WALLY.
explanation.definitionFit: An ally is someone on your side, an associate or partner in a shared effort.

clue.text: Defensive position of British PM falling short, intended to be heard

indicators.note: falling short means not reaching the end, so the final letter is lost

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for British
Clement Attlee was British Prime Minister 1945 to 1951

indicators.note: to be heard means we take the sound of the word, not its spelling

parts.note: intended means meant, and MENT sounds the same

explanation.surface: A British premier's failed plan to defend his position, made public.
explanation.walkthrough: ATTLEE loses its last E; Attlee was the Labour Prime Minister after the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: A battlement is the notched parapet on a castle wall, from which defenders fought.

clue.text: Monarch visiting school's grounds

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside a place, so one word enters the other

parts.note: read as schools, a verb: to school is to train
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword monarch

explanation.surface: The Queen tours a school's playing fields.
explanation.walkthrough: 'school's' is not a possessive: read it as schools, a verb meaning trains or teaches.
explanation.definitionFit: Terrains are tracts of land, so they can be called grounds.

clue.text: Most tricky ordeal in which one is faced with a bit of a dilemma?

indicators.note: in which says the other pieces are placed inside the word just named

parts.note: an ordeal is a severe test

indicators.note: being faced with something means having it in front, so that piece comes first

parts.note: a dilemma is said to have two horns
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: The hardest trial is one where you face a real dilemma.
explanation.walkthrough: The horns of a dilemma are its two equally bad options, so a horn is a bit of one.
explanation.definitionFit: Thorny means full of difficulty, so the thorniest problem is the most tricky one.

clue.text: Maker of ripples? A toothy reptile gobbles it

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something gobbled is swallowed whole, so it ends up inside the eater

parts.note: gator is short for alligator
taken as written

explanation.surface: An alligator splashing in the water while swallowing something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maker of ripples' suggests the reptile itself; the question mark flags a whimsical definition of a stirrer.
explanation.definitionFit: An agitator stirs up trouble, and literally an agitator is a paddle that stirs a liquid into ripples.

clue.text: Past Socialist turning Conservative becomes offensive

indicators.note: turning means facing the opposite way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: ago means in the past
a red is a socialist or communist
a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A former socialist defects to the Tories and turns nasty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning Conservative' reads as defecting, but turning reverses the two words before it while the Conservative piece stays forwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Derogatory remarks belittle or disparage someone, so they are offensive.

clue.text: Demonstrate again, bringing rebuke

definitions.meaning: first meaning: ..., establish a second time
second meaning: to scold or reprimand

explanation.surface: Showing someone again what they did wrong earns a telling-off.
explanation.definitionFit: To prove is to demonstrate, so re-prove is to do so again; reprove also means to scold someone.

clue.text: Go away, only half firing

indicators.note: keeping only half of a word means the rest of it is cut off

parts.note: firing a gun is shooting

explanation.surface: Leave, the gun is only half going off.
explanation.walkthrough: Keep the first four of the eight letters of SHOOTING.
explanation.definitionFit: Shoo is the exclamation used to drive someone off, an order meaning go away.

clue.text: One making lock secure?

parts.note: surface reading: a locksmith or a bolt fastening a door
setter's reading: a lock is a tress of hair, held in place by fine mesh

explanation.surface: Something that keeps a door lock fastened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lock' points to doors and keys; here it is a lock of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairnet is a fine mesh worn over the hair to keep the tresses in place.

clue.text: Sweet person of means starts to express emotion

parts.note: a toff is British slang for a rich, upper-class person

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters, so only those are kept

parts.note: the first letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A kind rich man begins to show his feelings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' reads as a description of the person; it is a noun, a confection.
explanation.definitionFit: Toffee is a chewy confection of boiled sugar and butter, a sweet in British usage.

clue.text: Firm facing endless shame to go under?

indicators.note: endless means the last letter is taken off the word
facing means standing in front of, so the first piece comes before the next

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm
a shame, as in what a shame, is a pity

explanation.surface: A company facing disgrace and ready to sink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go under' suggests a business failing, which suits the surface; here it means die.
explanation.definitionFit: Cop it is British slang for being killed or dying, and to go under can mean to perish.

clue.text: Reasons for rejecting upper-class eccentrics

indicators.note: rejecting something means throwing it out, so a letter is removed

parts.note: causes are reasons
U is the abbreviation for upper-class, and it is the letter dropped

explanation.surface: Why the posh dismiss oddballs.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop U from CAUSES. U for upper-class comes from 1950s British debate on U and non-U speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A case, in informal speech, is an odd or eccentric person, as in he's a real case.

clue.text: Turk? A national abroad

indicators.note: abroad means scattered widely, so the letters are spread into a new order

parts.note: the fodder, every letter used

explanation.surface: Is a Turk simply a national of his country living overseas?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as an example: not every Anatolian is a Turk.
explanation.definitionFit: Anatolia is the Asian heartland of Turkey, so a native of it is, by example, a Turk.

clue.text: Duck? Eager to eat it!

indicators.note: what is eaten goes inside the eater, so one word surrounds another

parts.note: eager means avid
it refers back to the duck, and a duck in cricket is a score of nought, the letter O

explanation.surface: A duck that is greedy to gobble up its food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' looks like the bird, and also stands for the O that 'it' points back to; as the definition it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To duck a question or a blow is to dodge or evade it.

clue.text: Switching off, making room for love and silence

indicators.note: making room for something means opening a space so it can be put inside

parts.note: a shutdown is the switching off of a machine or plant
love is zero in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: Turning things off clears space for love and quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Switching off' looks like the definition but is the wordplay; the definition is the verb at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To shout down a speaker is to stop them being heard by noise, a phrasal verb meaning to silence.

clue.text: Criminal division on the home front?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a criminal who receives and sells stolen goods
second meaning: a barrier dividing the garden in front of a house

explanation.surface: A wartime crook at work behind the lines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home front' sounds like wartime civilian life; here it is just the front garden of a home.
explanation.definitionFit: A receiver of stolen property is called a fence, and a fence is also a garden boundary or partition.

clue.text: Transfixed, like an extra on stage?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: pierced right through with a pointed weapon
second meaning, playful: holding a spear, as the walk-on spear carriers in a play do

explanation.surface: Riveted to the spot, like a nervous bit-part actor.
explanation.walkthrough: A spear carrier is a theatre's term for a minor walk-on role; the question mark flags the made-up sense of armed with a spear.
explanation.definitionFit: Speared means pierced by a lance, and fancifully equipped with one, as a stage extra often is.

clue.text: A few lines from the Home Counties that may stand

parts.note: the Home Counties are those around London, in the South East of England
stet is the proofreader's mark meaning let it stand

explanation.surface: Some verses from the commuter belt that are worth keeping.
explanation.walkthrough: The Home Counties are the counties surrounding London, abbreviated as SE for South East.
explanation.definitionFit: A sestet is a group of six lines of verse, such as the last six of a sonnet.
